expectations.text: Names the Osborne effect as the specific risk of announcing an unshipped successor while still selling the current version
expectations.evidence: "It's an Osborne-effect setup against your own installed base."

expectations.text: Explains the mechanism: buyers defer or cancel purchases of the shipping product once its successor is announced
expectations.evidence: "A page that says 'v3 GA — Q4' tells every one of them, and every prospect currently evaluating v2, to wait."

expectations.text: Cites the Osborne Computer Corporation 1983 precedent - prototype successors announced, dealers cancelled orders for the shipping machine, sales collapsed
expectations.evidence: "The Osborne Computer Corporation collapsed this way in 1983: announcing the successor killed sales of the shipping product, before the successor existed to replace it."

expectations.text: Gives the rule: publish direction and sequencing, and attach dates only to work already shipping
expectations.evidence: "Direction and sequencing, no dates ... Only put a real date on something already shipping."

expectations.text: Rejects the page as drafted, specifically the dated Q2/Q3/Q4 entries for unshipped work
expectations.evidence: "Verdict: don't publish it as specified." ... "Q2/Q3/Q4 promises on work that hasn't started don't belong on the same page as work that has."

expectations.text: If a roadmap is published anyway, requires explicit non-commitment language modelled on GitHub's public roadmap: subject to change, not a commitment guarantee obligation or promise, and not to be relied on for purchasing decisions
expectations.evidence: "following the pattern GitHub uses on its own public roadmap ... Every item carries the standard disclaimer: subject to change, not a commitment, don't buy against this timeline. Put it in writing, not just in spirit."

expectations.text: Classifies roadmap dates as a grey zone requiring a decision recorded in the charter rather than a reflex
expectations.evidence: The transcript contains no charter document and no explicit 'grey zone' classification language for roadmap dates.

expectations.text: Warns that a roadmap detailed enough to be useful can read as competitor intelligence
expectations.evidence: No mention of competitor intelligence risk from roadmap detail; the harms discussed are buyer deferral, cloud-vs-self-hosted trust, and credibility loss from missed dates.

expectations.text: States that missed dates cost more credibility than the announced feature earns
expectations.evidence: "When it slips ... you haven't shown buyers you're serious, you've shown them your public promises don't hold, which is the opposite of what marketing is trying to buy."

expectations.text: Answers the enterprise-buyer motive with evidence a company evaluator actually uses - release cadence, response times, security handling, maintenance capacity - instead of dated promises
expectations.evidence: "What convinces an approver is evidence the vendor is alive, responsive, and disciplined right now: release cadence, how you handle security issues, how fast you respond, what you've already shipped and why."
